title: Moby-Dick Ch. 2 — The Carpet-Bag: Action Spine
adaptation_principle: Reduce the chapter to the concrete decisions and path-changes: delayed passage, frugal search for lodging, mistaken church entry and retreat, and resolving to try the Spouter Inn.
action_oriented_synopsis: Ishmael reaches New Bedford on a bitter Saturday night and discovers the Nantucket packet has sailed, delaying him until Monday. Needing food and a bed, he chooses frugality, searches the dark streets, and rejects the bright, expensive inns while heading waterward. Mistaking a smoky doorway for an inn, he blunders into a church service and quickly backs out. He finds the Spouter Inn, deems its ominous sign cheap enough, and resolves to go in.

caption_spine: I arrived in New Bedford on a Saturday night in December, only to learn the Nantucket packet had already sailed, and I must wait till Monday.
Sounding my pocket and finding only a few pieces of silver, I paced the dreary streets, shunned the jolly, costly houses, and steered waterward for the cheapest lodgings.
Taking a smoky light for a public house, I stumbled in, opened an inner door upon a negro church, and muttering, backed out from that wretched entertainment.

At last I spied the swinging sign of the Spouter Inn—Peter Coffin—ominous names; yet here, thought I, is the very spot for cheap lodgings—let us scrape the ice from our frosted feet and see what sort of a place this may be.

Much was I disappointed upon learning that the little packet for Nantucket had already sailed, and that no way of reaching that place would offer, till the following Monday.

With halting steps I paced the streets, and passed the sign of “The Crossed Harpoons”—but it looked too expensive and jolly there.
Further on, from the bright red windows of the “Sword-Fish Inn,” there came such fervent rays...
I now by instinct followed the streets that took me waterward, for there, doubtless, were the cheapest, if not the cheeriest inns.

source_evidence: I at last came to a dim sort of light not far from the docks, and heard a forlorn creaking in the air; and looking up, saw a swinging sign over the door with a white painting upon it, faintly representing a tall straight jet of misty spray, and these words underneath—“The Spouter Inn:—Peter Coffin.”
Coffin?—Spouter?—Rather ominous in that particular connexion, thought I.
I thought that here was the very spot for cheap lodgings, and the best of pea coffee.
Let us scrape the ice from our frosted feet, and see what sort of a place this “Spouter” may be.
